passage: Trisha, come and sit. I hear someone told you girls can't play cricket. Let me tell you something. I'm Deepika, your Masi. When I was ten I loved cricket. The boys in our lane said, "Girls don't play, go and skip." It felt so unfair that my chest went hot. But I still went every evening with my bat and stood at the edge of the lane. I asked my father why there was such a rule. He said, "It's how it's always been." I said, "That's not a reason." One day a boy called Imran said, "Let her bowl one." Months later, they had stopped saying it. Keep your bat, Trisha.

qa.q: What did the boys in Deepika's lane say to her?
qa.a: They said, "Girls don't play, go and skip."

qa.q: What did ten-year-old Deepika feel when the boys said girls don't play?
qa.a: She felt angry at how unfair it was, so much that her chest went hot.

qa.q: What did Deepika do that Trisha could also do?
qa.a: She kept doing what she loved, turned up every evening, and asked why the rule existed.

qa.q: How did Deepika's father see her question about the rule?
qa.a: He offered no reason beyond how it had always been, which suggests he had not thought about why the rule exists.

grounding: A girl told girls should not play cricket feels it is unfair, keeps playing and asks why the rule exists, told by an elder.

passage:
"Asif, are you crying? Over a football match?" Anirban laughed. "Boys don't cry, yaar."
Asif wiped his face fast. "I'm not crying. It's sweat."
"Sweat from your eyes?"
"We lost the final by one goal! I missed the penalty!"
"So? My dad says crying is for girls."
Asif sat down on the bench. "Why, though? Who made that rule?"
Anirban opened his mouth, then shut it. "I don't know. Everyone says it."
"My Abbu cried when my baby sister was born. He's not weak."
Anirban scuffed the ground. "Okay. I cried when my dog died. Don't tell anyone."
"I won't." Asif laughed wetly. "Next year we'll win and cry about that too."
"Deal," Anirban said, and sat down beside him.

qa.q: By how much did they lose the final?
Why did Asif say it was just sweat?
qa.a: He felt embarrassed about crying after Anirban laughed at him.

qa.q: What did Asif do that challenged the rule?
qa.a: He asked who made the rule and pointed out that his Abbu cried and is not weak.

qa.q: How did Anirban's view change during the talk?
qa.a: He realised he did not know why the rule existed, admitted he had cried too, and sat beside Asif.

grounding: A boy told that boys should not cry questions who made the rule and finds a friend who accepts him.

passage:
I'm Payal, and last summer our building's cricket team needed a bowler. I've been bowling at the wall since I was small. But when I walked onto the terrace pitch, Sharma Uncle from the fourth floor called out, "Cricket is for boys, beti. Go and play with the girls."
My face went hot. It felt so unfair. I bowl faster than half of them!
I almost went home. Then Manoj, the captain, tossed me the ball. "Uncle, just watch one over."
I took three wickets. Sharma Uncle clapped, a bit grudgingly.
That night I asked Mummy why people say that. She said some rules are just old habits nobody ever questioned. I'm still bowling. I'm the team's opening bowler now.

qa.q: How many wickets did Payal take in the over?
How did Payal feel when Sharma Uncle said cricket is for boys?
qa.a: Hurt and angry; it felt unfair, and Payal's face went hot.

qa.q: What helped Payal keep doing what Payal loves?
qa.a: Manoj's support, proving it in one over, and asking Mummy why people say such things.

qa.q: How might Sharma Uncle have seen things after the over?
qa.a: He had to admit Payal could play, clapping even if grudgingly.

grounding: A girl told that cricket is for boys feels it is unfair, keeps playing with a friend's support and asks why the rule exists.
